analysis.one_liner: Orders a government study of grocery price increases and ideas for lowering them.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill asking for a federal study of grocery prices was introduced in June 2024 and never received any committee action or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Despite its name, the bill would not set prices or cap anything. It directs the Government Accountability Office — Congress's nonpartisan investigative office — to study how the consumer price index for food eaten at home has changed over the past 20 years, and to report within 180 days on the findings plus recommendations to help lower grocery costs for consumers. The report would go to three congressional committees and carry no force of law.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary grocery shoppers, who are the stated beneficiaries: the bill is designed to produce an official, nonpartisan diagnosis of why food-at-home prices have climbed and a list of recommended policy fixes. Members of Congress would also gain a document they could cite in future legislation, though the bill itself changes nothing.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Comptroller General to study changes in the Consumer Price Index for food at home over a 20-year period ending at enactment, plus any other economic metrics needed to assess the impact of food costs on U.S. consumers [S2].

Requires the Comptroller General to submit a report to specified House and Senate committees within 180 days of enactment containing the study's findings and recommendations to help lower food-at-home costs for consumers [S2].

The bill was introduced by Rep. Marcus Molinaro with initial cosponsors Reps. Ryan, Ciscomani, and Davis of North Carolina, and drew a bipartisan cosponsor list of 5 members (4 Democrats, 1 Republican) [S1] [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the normal operating budget of the Government Accountability Office, which would absorb the staff time to run the study and write the report. No company, industry, or household pays anything directly, and no new programs or price rules are funded.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no policy: it authorizes only a study and nonbinding recommendations, so even if enacted and followed perfectly, grocery prices would not fall because of this bill [S2].

It is titled the 'Lower Grocery Prices Act' but its only operative provisions direct a retrospective study of 20 years of price index data, which risks implying more action than the bill actually contains [S1] [S2].

The report would go to the House Energy and Commerce, House Financial Services, and Senate Finance committees rather than the Agriculture committees with direct jurisdiction over food policy, an odd routing that could limit its usefulness [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is trivial — a GAO study uses existing staff and budget — but so is the benefit. GAO studies of this kind are genuinely useful for building later legislation and putting an official record under industry pricing, yet a study alone does not lower a single price. The bill is best understood as a first step or a messaging vehicle rather than relief for squeezed grocery budgets, and the grand title overstates what it does.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2024, referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcus Molinaro introduced the bill on June 28, 2024, joined on introduction by Reps. Ryan, Ciscomani, and Davis of North Carolina [S1] [S2] [S4].
The same day it was introduced, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the bill's complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, vote, or floor consideration [S4].
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors — 4 Democrats and 1 Republican — showing bipartisan interest that never translated into committee activity [S3].
Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not passed by then expire, so the bill died without any vote being taken on it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill would only have ordered a study, nobody's grocery bill changes because it died. The groups best positioned under the status quo are the food and grocery companies whose pricing practices the study might have put under an official spotlight, since no report now exists to fuel legislation against them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one materially; food companies unaffected

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and drew cosponsors from both parties (4 of its 5 cosponsors were Democrats), and nothing in the record shows opposition on party grounds — it simply never moved.

industries.industry: Grocery retailers and packaged food manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would not regulate, fine, or cap anything in the food industry; its only realistic effect is a government report examining 20 years of grocery price data, which could spotlight industry pricing and feed future legislation. Because the bill never advanced, the industry's position is unchanged.
The bill would add one more study to the GAO's workload using its existing appropriations, giving the agency a mandate on a topic of broad public concern. The cost to taxpayers is minimal.
